newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says can't predict Lebanon detainees' fate.
newsitem.headline: Japan says can't predict Lebanon detainees' fate.

text.p: Japan's top police officer said on Thursday he believed Japanese Red Army guerrillas were being held in Lebanon but it was impossible to predict whether the detainees would be returned to their homeland.
"It is unpredictable whether they would be handed over to Japan," Takaji Kunimatsu, head of the National Police Agency, told a news conference.
Lebanese government and security officials surprised Japan on Monday by denying they were holding any suspected Red Army members, contrary to what had been widely reported last week.
But Kunimatsu said he believed that Japanese Red Army members were indeed being detained in Lebanon.
"There are people who have various ideas within the Lebanese government," he said.
"But if they belatedely say 'There are no Japanese Red Army members (being held)', we can't back down and say 'Is that so'."
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo on February 18 that Lebanese authorities had told him they had arrested up to six Red Army members in the eastern Bekaa Valley.

On Tuesday, Japan asked Lebanese authorities to let its diplomats meet those who were reported to be held in Beirut on suspicion of belonging to the Japanese Red Army, Lebanese diplomatic sources said.
Japanese ambassador to Lebanon Yasuji Ishikagi made the request but did not receive any confirmation on the identities of those reported to be detained.
"We hope the Lebanese government will appropriately deal with the situation and Japan is waiting for contacts from the Lebanese government for any further development," Hashimoto said on Thursday.
Syria, which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon, controls the Bekaa valley where some of the guerrilla suspects were said to have been arrested.

The Red Army, founded in 1971, is allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions. The Bekaa Valley was a haven during Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war for guerrilla groups including Lebanese Moslems and Marxists, Palestinians, Kurds and the Japanese Red Army.
